Key takeaways

  • We introduce PuzzleMixEscape, a benchmark of 94 interactive 3D escape-room levels for multimodal large language models. Within a single environment, models must explore to find clues, reason through puzzles, and manipulate objects to escape.
  • We propose a pipeline for constructing interactive levels and a memory method, CoordMem, for long-horizon puzzle solving. The pipeline adapts puzzles from public escape-room materials into 3D levels and provides an executable reference solution for each one. CoordMem separates memory updates from action selection, supplying information relevant to the current step before each decision.
  • We evaluate six multimodal large language models across six capability dimensions and find that the gap between models and human players widens as levels become more difficult. GPT-6-astra, the strongest model overall across the four difficulty groups, escaped from 97.4% of Easy levels but only 9.1% of Hard levels. Further analysis shows that models make progress on individual puzzles but struggle to complete a series of interdependent stages.

Overview

Can multimodal large language models bring exploration, reasoning, and action together to escape a room? PuzzleMixEscape investigates this question through 94 interactive 3D escape rooms. Starting from a first-person view, each model decides where to go, what to inspect, and how to use the objects it finds. By varying how hard the clues are to find and how complex the puzzles are to solve, we test whether models can act on earlier discoveries and ultimately open the exit.

We evaluated six multimodal large language models across four difficulty groups and compared their performance with that of human players. GPT-6-astra, the strongest model overall, achieved a 97.4% escape rate on Easy, close to human performance in that group. On Hard, its escape rate fell to 9.1%.

1. Introduction

Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) perform well on visual understanding and reasoning tasks and are increasingly used in interactive environments. Unlike question answering on static images or videos, interactive tasks do not provide all relevant information upfront. Models must actively gather visual information, reason about it, and act to reach a goal. Evaluation must therefore test both how well models interpret observations and how effectively they act on them over multiple steps.

Existing benchmarks only partially meet this requirement. A first group evaluates spatial understanding and puzzle-style reasoning on pre-supplied observations, such as videos, multiple images, or puzzle images. Because all observations are given in advance and evaluation mainly measures answer correctness, these benchmarks cannot assess whether models can actively acquire missing information. A second group places models in interactive environments, where they act on sequential observations, change viewpoints or manipulate objects to reveal hidden information, or combine historical observations with newly acquired ones. However, these settings place different demands on exploration and puzzle solving, motivating evaluation under different combinations of the two. This raises a natural question: can MLLMs reliably combine spatial understanding with physical interaction when later actions depend on earlier discoveries?

Escape rooms are well suited to studying this question. To escape, a player must explore the space, collect clues and items, solve puzzles that draw on different kinds of reasoning, and carry earlier findings forward to later stages, so these capabilities must work together rather than be tested in isolation. Yet existing escape-room benchmarks capture only part of this picture. Text-based escape-room benchmarks test whether agents can infer how to use and combine tools from written descriptions, but do not require them to discover clues visually. Image-based benchmarks test whether agents can interpret visual clues and decide what to inspect, but restrict exploration to predefined views. Interactive 3D benchmarks let agents navigate rooms and manipulate objects directly, but their standard tasks primarily vary prop dependencies and cue conditions rather than offering a wide range of puzzle-solving mechanisms.

To fill this gap, we introduce PuzzleMixEscape, a 3D escape-room benchmark for MLLMs that covers active perception and exploration, spatial reasoning, physical interaction reasoning, long-horizon task planning, numerical computation and mathematical reasoning, and logical and commonsense reasoning. In each level, a model explores the scene from a first-person view, inspects objects to collect clues and items, infers the solution, and acts by using items and operating devices, updating its reasoning as the environment changes until it escapes. Some levels require connecting clues from different areas or reusing earlier information at later stages. The levels differ in their underlying puzzle solutions rather than in surface features such as room appearance, passcodes, or item names, so they cannot be solved with a fixed template. We build them with a pipeline that adapts puzzle designs from public escape-room game materials into interactive 3D tasks, each with a reference solution.

2. Benchmark design

2.1 Task design

Task setting. In each level of PuzzleMixEscape, the model starts with a first-person view of a 3D scene and must find a way out. It can move, look around, and interact with objects to uncover clues and test possible solutions.

Exploration difficulty. Exploration difficulty concerns how hard it is to find and reach the relevant clues and objects. They may be clustered in one area, or spread across connected rooms that the model must revisit as it gains access to new areas or finds new items.

Puzzle complexity. Puzzle complexity concerns what the model must do once it has the evidence. A simple puzzle may require applying a single clue directly, whereas a more complex one may require combining several clues, using a tool under specific conditions, or carrying an intermediate result forward to a later stage.

Difficulty groups. We organize levels into four groups based on exploration difficulty and puzzle complexity. Easy and Medium-A use relatively simple puzzles with limited and more extensive exploration, respectively. Medium-B and Hard use more complex puzzles, again with limited and more extensive exploration, respectively.

2.2 Data analysis

PuzzleMixEscape comprises 94 levels across four difficulty groups. The ring shows the category shares reported in the paper. The center gives the independent puzzle count across all 94 levels. We also count object instances by difficulty group. Across all four groups, there are 3,081 object instances, averaging 32.8 per level. We relate exploration scope, measured by the number of distinct rooms involved in solving a level, to puzzle dependency depth, the number of stages in its longest prerequisite chain.

3. Method

Long-horizon puzzle solving in PuzzleMixEscape requires models to remember earlier clues, track changes in object states, and avoid repeating failed attempts. We introduce CoordMem, a memory method that separates memory updates from action selection. A dedicated memory agent maintains the memory for each episode: before each action, it receives the existing memory, the current first-person view, and the last action and its feedback, and proposes additions, updates, or archival operations, each citing supporting images or feedback. A puzzle-solving agent then chooses the next action from the updated memory and current view. The memory has four parts: Map, Clues, Pending Tasks, and Attempts.

4. Result

4.1 Main result

4.1.1 How large is the gap between models and humans?

The results indicate that models lag substantially behind human players across all metrics. This gap widens with level difficulty: the strongest model, GPT-6-astra, approaches human performance on Easy levels, but as levels require longer chains of interdependent puzzles, its escape rate collapses, falling from 97.4% on Easy to 9.1% on Hard. Hint use follows the same trend, and even frequent hints could not offset the difficulty of the hardest levels. Notably, models still reached a substantial share of checkpoints on levels they failed to escape, suggesting that their main weakness lies not in getting started but in sustaining progress through the full sequence of puzzles.

4.1.2 How much do hints help with puzzle solving?

Whether a hint helped depended on both the model and the puzzle type. GPT-6-astra and GPT-6.1-sol solved all mathematical puzzles without hints and 77% and 91% of hinted exploration and logic puzzles, likely because failures there stem from missing information that a hint can directly supply. The other four models solved 55% of hinted exploration puzzles but only 32% in logic, since a hint supplies information but not reasoning. Even for the two strongest models, hints were far less effective in spatial reasoning and physical interaction, where knowing what to do is not enough: the model must still judge positions and orientations or anticipate how objects will respond.

4.1.3 Can models carry out multi-step plans?

The model struggled to solve tasks requiring several interdependent steps, even when provided with hints. Long-horizon planning was the weakest category for nearly every model: GPT-6-astra and GPT-6.1-sol solved only 57.3% and 54.6% of planning puzzles, and the remaining models at most 38.2%, with hints offering little improvement. Because each step in these puzzles depends on the outcome of earlier ones, an early mistake blocks all later progress, and a hint that clarifies one step cannot restore the rest of the sequence. This points to a core limitation in maintaining a coherent multi-step plan rather than in solving individual steps.

4.2 Ablation study

We compared three ways of providing memory to the puzzle-solving agent: no CoordMem, the full memory record, and a subset selected by the memory agent before each action. Across the three models, providing the full record left the mean escape rate unchanged at 52.9%. Selecting what to pass on raised it to 57.1% and improved checkpoint coverage and puzzle solve rate by 6.8 and 6.4 percentage points, respectively, over the baseline without CoordMem.

The full record helped some models but hindered others. GPT-6-astra escaped more often with full memory, while GPT-6.1-terra and Qwen-3.8-Max escaped less often. For Terra, the puzzle solve rate fell from 63.6% without CoordMem to 60.5% with full memory, but rose to 71.0% with selective memory. This suggests that, for some models, finding the relevant clue in memory can be harder than using it once it has been selected.

4.3 Further analysis

4.3.1 How do paths differ between successful and failed runs?

Failed runs lingered near a clue about twice as long, averaging 29.3 steps and about 17 interactions within 1 m, compared with 14.5 steps and about 8 interactions in successful runs. Thus, the models’ main limitation lies not in locating clues but in working out how to use them.

4.3.2 Do models with higher escape rates also perform better across puzzle types?

GPT-6-astra and GPT-6.1-sol had the highest escape rates and ranked at or near the top on all six puzzle types. Their advantage was not confined to one or two specialties: even on their weaker puzzle types, they remained competitive. Within each difficulty group, models that escaped more often also interacted with objects more successfully.

4.3.3 How often do object interactions succeed by accident?

We used GPT-6.1-sol to compare each model’s stated intent with the outcome of its successful take and use actions, excluding cases where the evidence was insufficient. No model succeeded on more than 50.3% of take attempts or 39.2% of use attempts. Yet for every model, more than 85% of assessable successes matched the intended outcome for both actions. This suggests that failures often came from misjudging what an action required rather than from choosing actions at random.

4.3.4 Can models spot and correct failures from vision alone?

We removed the text feedback that normally tells a model when an action fails. With only visual feedback, the escape rate fell from 60.0% to 42.9% for GPT-6.1-sol and from 20.0% to 2.9% for Qwen-3.8-Max. Across the seven failure types, the models noticed only 28.9–57.9% of failed actions. When they did notice a failure, however, they adjusted their next action in 90.0–100% of cases. Thus, the models’ weakness lies in perceiving failures from visual observations rather than in responding to them.

4.3.5 Can models solve the same puzzles in text, images, and rooms?

We presented the same benchmark-style math and logic puzzles as text, an image, and a room with clues spread across the scene. Models consistently performed best on text, lower on images, and lowest in rooms. Most room failures involved puzzles the same model had solved in both other forms. Thus, models that can solve a puzzle often fail to find its clues and act on them in the room, a gap between knowing and doing that PuzzleMixEscape exposes but static reasoning benchmarks cannot measure.
